---
title: "Slides"
---

Lecture slides and notes will be linked here as the semester proceeds.

- [Linear Model Prediction Methods](predictionOLS26.qmd) — prediction and quantities of interest in the linear model (at-means and average effects; ML, delta, and simulation-based uncertainty), previewing the methods we generalize to nonlinear models.
- [Binary Response Models](binarymodels26.qmd) — building a maximum-likelihood model for a binary outcome: why the linear probability model fails, the latent-variable and random-utility motivations, the likelihood and link functions, and interpretation via predicted probabilities, marginal effects, and odds.
- [Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics](likelihood26.qmd) — what a likelihood is and how it differs from a probability; the estimation machine and how little of it changes from one model to the next; analytic methods and closed-form solutions, and where they fail; and the two derivatives — the score and the Hessian — that locate the estimate and set its standard error.
- [Maximizing the Log-Likelihood Function](llfmax26.qmd) — Newton–Raphson from the ground up: where the method comes from, what its two halves do, one step worked by hand, then the whole loop run to convergence on a real logit, with an animated climb, the iteration log, starting values, and the properties that justify the estimator.
- [Prediction Methods for MLE Models](prediction26.qmd) — quantities of interest from nonlinear models: at-means and average effects, building a scenario's linear prediction, King–Tomz–Wittenberg simulation, ML and delta-method standard errors with end-point transformation, the bootstrap, average effects bounded two ways, and guidance on which approach and which technique to choose.
- [Diagnostics, Classification, and Fit](binaryextensions126.qmd) — what to check after a binary-response model is fitted: whether the link's symmetry assumption suits the data, how classification and ROC curves work and why they mean more for a House roll call than for democratic peace models, how separation breaks the estimator (especially when you add fixed effects), rare-events bias and the Firth correction, and the trinity of tests with the information criteria.
